title: Losing Control Of Your Class? Here's How To Get It Back
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin frames a deteriorating classroom as an opportunity to hit reset rather than a crisis to endure. He recommends starting the reset first thing in the morning, rearranging seating, cleaning up physical clutter, and blocking out at least a full hour to methodically rebuild expectations. That hour is spent re-modeling routines and procedures from scratch, with special emphasis on practicing walking in line as the fastest way to restore focus, then reintroducing the classroom management plan as if it were the first day of school. He also calls for teachers to personally recommit and openly acknowledge to students that accountability had lapsed. The piece insists that responsibility for a slipping classroom always lies with the teacher's own consistency, not with the students.
points: A slipping classroom can always be deliberately reset rather than allowed to deteriorate further.
Physical changes - new seating arrangements and a decluttered room - signal to students that expectations are changing.
Blocking out at least a full hour to re-model and re-practice routines, especially walking in line, rebuilds focus quickly.
Reintroducing the classroom management plan as if it were the first day of school resets accountability.
Responsibility for a classroom losing control always rests with the teacher's consistency, not the students.
quotes: One of the happy truths about classroom management is that you can always press the restart button. You can always call a do-over.
Don’t wait until your students are climbing the walls, and you’re sobbing during your lunch break. Do it now.
A new place to sit signals to students that change is in the air. The old way of doing things isn’t in play any longer.
Clutter, on the other hand, whispers to all who enter your classroom, “Mediocre will do.
Although all procedures are important, walking in line is at the top of the list. Nothing focuses students faster or more effectively than practicing a smooth, brisk, arrow-straight line.

Whenever you feel like you’re losing control of your classroom, it’s because of something you’re doing–or not doing. It’s not about your students. It never has been and it never will be. It’s about you.
Effective classroom management is a daily, hourly, commitment. As soon as you let up and relax your standards, you’re going to pay for it–with interest.
